Positive Contribution: The FY26 annual report says Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions intensity of the Net Zero 2030 target portfolio is 45% below the FY16 baseline, and that 31.3 MW of solar capacity was installed across 17 centres at 30 June 2026.
Negative Contribution: Vicinity's 2024 modern slavery statement says a Cleaning Accountability Framework audit in FY23 found issues at Carlingford Court relating to health and safety, workload and pay.
Evidence: Paraphrase of the annual report for the year ended 30 June 2025. The statement states the audit findings and that they were remediated.

SDG: SDG 7, 9, 12 and 13, named in the strategy section. The 2025 integrated report also prints SDG 8 and SDG 15. The company responsibility page prints the headings SDG 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 15, 16 and 17.
Activity: Electricity generation, mainly hydropower, with wind, solar and thermal generation, plus green hydrogen.
Positive Contribution: About 86% of electricity generated in 2025 came from hydropower. The strategy section also describes wind, solar and green hydrogen. The 2025 integrated report says ETS emissions were 0.85 million tonnes of CO2 in 2025, 78% below the 3.8 million tonnes of 2005, and that 25,370 GWh were generated from hydropower.
Negative Contribution: The same generation table reports thermal power as under 7% of 2025 electricity. The fuel of those plants is not settled here. E-Control case 06/21 says the Vienna magistrate imposed a final administrative fine of 1,000 euros, plus 10% of the procedural costs, on each managing director of Verbund Energy4Business GmbH for a late and ineffective REMIT disclosure of a plant shutdown. The 2025 integrated annual report says the Mellach combined-cycle gas turbine and the Mellach district-heating plant are deployed as necessary in gas operation. Thermal generation was 2,054 GWh in 2025, of which the combined-cycle plant was 2,052 GWh. The climate page says hard-coal use ended in 2020. VERBUND holds 51% of Gas Connect Austria, a natural-gas transmission operator. The report does not state those gas activities as a share of sales.
Evidence: Climate-friendly hydropower is the most important source of energy for our electricity generation.

SDG: SDG 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 13, 15 and 17. The company page prints a heading for each of these eight goals. The page says eight goals were identified.
Activity: Owns, lets and manages residential property in Germany, Austria and Sweden, and develops new homes for its own portfolio and for sale.
Positive Contribution: The 2025 sustainability statement prints German housing-stock carbon intensity of 31.2 and 30.7 kg CO2e per square metre, a change of -1.4%.
Negative Contribution: Reuters reported on 24 May 2021 that Vonovia and Deutsche Wohnen had agreed an 18 billion euro combination while tenant groups in Berlin were campaigning against large landlords, and that the companies offered to limit regular rent increases.
Evidence: Vonovia’s business model is based on the provision and rental of good-quality and, most importantly, affordable living space at the right time, as well as the management of these properties. The September article states the 56 percent and 39 percent figures and names Vonovia.
Source: Vonovia SE, Annual Report 2024, The Company, https://report.vonovia.com/2024/q4/en/the-company Reuters, 24 May 2021, https://www.reuters.com/business/germanys-biggest-landlords-agree-22-bln-merger-2021-05-25/. Reuters, 27 September 2021, https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/berliners-vote-expropriate-large-landlords-non-binding-referendum-2021-09-27/. Vonovia 2025 sustainability statement, https://report.vonovia.com/2025/q4/app/uploads/Vonovia_SE_Annual_Report_2025-Sustainability-Statement.pdf.
Controversy: On 27 September 2021 Reuters reported that about 56 percent of Berlin voters backed a non-binding referendum to expropriate large landlords, including Vonovia and Deutsche Wohnen, and that about 39 percent voted against. Vonovia's chief executive, Rolf Buch, said expropriation does not solve Berlin's housing problems. The vote did not itself transfer any homes.
Positive: The stated business is the provision and rental of affordable living space, together with housing-related services.

SDG: The 2025 corporate responsibility report does not print a goal numeral.
Activity: Medicines for serious diseases. The 2025 Form 10-K says Vertex creates medicines for specialty markets and names cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia among the approved uses.
Positive Contribution: The 2025 corporate responsibility report says absolute Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse-gas emissions were 49% below 2014. The report does not print a goal numeral.
Negative Contribution: In its final cystic-fibrosis report, the Institute for Clinical and Economic Review set a health-benefit price benchmark for Trikafta of $67,900 to $85,500 a year. It said that range required a discount of at least 73 percent from the list price, and it issued an Access and Affordability Alert.
Evidence: Paraphrase of the business description in the 2025 Form 10-K. The release states the benchmark range and the 73 percent discount.
Source: Vertex Pharmaceuticals Incorporated, Form 10-K for the year ended 31 December 2025, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/875320/000087532026000056/vrtx-20251231.htm. SDG: SDG 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 15 and 17. The 2026 SDG note says the board confirmed the strategic goals in 2020 and prints the official titles rather than the numerals: affordable, reliable, sustainable and modern energy; resilient infrastructure and innovation; inclusive, safe and resilient cities; decent work and economic growth; sustainable consumption and production; terrestrial ecosystems and forests; the global partnership; and urgent climate action.
Activity: Timberlands and wood products. The 2024 CDP response says the company owns or controls about 10.5 million acres of timberlands in the United States and manages about 14 million acres under long-term licences in Canada.
Positive Contribution: The same response says those timberlands are managed under sustainable forestry standards, and records a timber-products volume of 51,301,000 metric tons. The same note says more than two-thirds of Weyerhaeuser's own energy needs are met with renewable biomass from manufacturing by-products, and that the near-term target is to reduce Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse-gas emissions by 42% by 2030 against a 2020 baseline.
Negative Contribution: The Associated Press reported that Weyerhaeuser agreed to pay $600,000 to the Columbia River Restoration Fund after a settlement with Columbia Riverkeeper over alleged breaches of Washington water-quality law at Longview. The company denied that it had broken the law. It must also reroute a stormwater pipe. The Justice Department said the United States and Pennsylvania alleged that Weyerhaeuser modified and operated two coal-fired boilers at its Johnsonburg mill without required pollution-control upgrades and without permits limiting sulfur dioxide.
Evidence: Paraphrase of the 2024 CDP climate response. The response does not number an SDG. The AP report states the $600,000 payment and the company's denial. The Justice Department release states the PCB payment. The release states the $900,000 payment and that liability was not admitted.

Controversy: Each later violation under that agreement costs $5,000. An earlier Justice Department settlement, announced on 3 January 2005, required Weyerhaeuser to clean up the Plainwell mill and landfill on the Kalamazoo River and to pay $6.2 million toward PCB cleanup plus about $138,000 of EPA costs. That settlement did not resolve the rest of the river or natural-resource damages. On 22 July 2004 the department lodged a proposed consent decree. Weyerhaeuser agreed to pay $900,000, of which $675,000 would go to the United States and $225,000 to Pennsylvania, and did not admit liability. The release said the decree still needed public comment and court approval.
